paper_metadata.title: Hybrid Quantum Neural Networks with Amplitude Encoding for Credit Recovery Rate Prediction

summary: The paper studies a hybrid QML regressor for credit recovery-rate prediction on 1,725 observations with 256 features, using 8 qubits for amplitude encoding and a strongly entangling PQC. The main noiseless simulator result is RMSE 0.228 for amplitude encoding versus 0.242 for angle encoding and 0.246 for the classical FNN, while XGBoost is still best in four-fold CV at RMSE 0.222. A preliminary real-hardware test on Rigetti Ankaa-3 uses 5 qubits, 100 samples, 32 features, and 13 epochs, but it is explicitly presented as early-stage and not conclusive.

experiments.description: Hybrid quantum machine learning model for recovery rate prediction using classical preprocessing followed by amplitude encoding and a strongly entangling parameterized quantum circuit, evaluated against a classical feedforward neural network and XGBoost on a 256-feature credit recovery dataset.

algorithm.variant: hybrid QNN with amplitude encoding and strongly entangling PQC

problem_formulation.encoding_details: 256 classical features are encoded into an 8-qubit quantum state via amplitude encoding; the paper states N=2^n and uses 256 features -> 8 qubits
problem_formulation.objective_function: Regression objective minimizing RMSE for recovery rate prediction

problem_instance.description: Predict bond recovery rate (price 30 days after default) for defaulted bonds using firm-level, bond-level, credit-risk, categorical, and macroeconomic features.
problem_instance.dataset_name: NRF Research Project UP5 / CRI recovery rate dataset

dataset_specification.description: 1,725 observations from 576 firms spanning 1996-2023; recovery rate defined as bond price 30 days after default; 256 features from Bloomberg, Refinitiv, FRED, and CRI

problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: Continuous features standardized with z-score normalization using training-set statistics only; categorical True/False features mapped to 0/1; no missing values in retained variables; no PCA; fold-specific preprocessing to avoid leakage
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Four-fold cross-validation and leave-one-out cross-validation; RMSE tracked per epoch; Diebold-Mariano significance tests across folds and epochs

implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: Classical preprocessing layer with input and hidden layer of equal size using LeakyReLU (slope -0.3)
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: Final classical output layer for regression; measurement expectation values of Z observables are passed to the classical head

convergence_data.loss_curve_shape: RMSE decreases over epochs; best average RMSE at epoch 55 for CV and 86 for LOOCV

speedup_claims.caveats: The paper reports better RMSE than the FNN and angle-encoding QML, but does not claim an asymptotic quantum speedup. It also notes that XGBoost can be faster in simulation and that runtime comparisons across GPU classical models and CPU-based quantum simulation are not meaningful.

complexity_analysis.quantum_complexity: Amplitude encoding state preparation via Möttönen protocol uses 2^(n+1)-3 elementary gates for n qubits; PQC parameter count scales as O(3 log2 N) for N features

advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: 8 qubits, state-vector simulation on CPU; amplitude encoding with Möttönen state preparation and a strongly entangling PQC
limiting_factors: No real-hardware benchmark for the main amplitude-encoding model
Classical XGBoost is slightly better in CV RMSE (0.222 vs 0.228)
Amplitude encoding state preparation is deep and data-loading heavy

notes: default.qubit state-vector simulator explicitly reported; no real QPU used for the main experiments.
8 qubits inferred directly from 256 features encoded as 2^n with n=8, and explicitly stated in the paper.
Circuit depth for the main amplitude-encoding experiment is not explicitly given; only gate-count scaling for the Möttönen protocol is reported.
Speedup order is not proven; paper discusses compact representation and parameter scaling but does not establish asymptotic quantum advantage over best classical methods.
Authors claim the amplitude-encoding QML is more accurate and stable than the FNN, but the strongest classical baseline (XGBoost) achieves lower CV RMSE.
Main experiment is noiseless simulation, not QPU execution.

problem_formulation.objective_function: Regression objective minimizing RMSE for recovery rate prediction

notes: default.qubit state-vector simulator explicitly reported; no real QPU used for the main experiments.
